analysis.one_liner: Ends tobacco companies' tax deductions for legal-settlement payments and puts the added revenue into NIH health research.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 1997 with no cosponsors, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When tobacco companies pay billions to federal or state governments under court judgments or settlements, the tax code treats those payments like any other business expense and lets the companies deduct them from taxable income. This bill would have ended that deduction and deposited the resulting new federal revenue into a dedicated trust fund for National Institutes of Health research, including work on reducing tobacco use.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state treasuries would collect more tax revenue from tobacco companies, and the National Institutes of Health would receive a dedicated funding stream for medical research, including research on women's health, minority health, AIDS, and programs to reduce tobacco use.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code so that no deduction is allowed for any payment to federal, state, or local governments under a tobacco judgment or settlement, including the proposed June 20, 1997 national tobacco settlement [S3].

The net revenue gain from removing the deduction would be automatically appropriated to a new NIH Trust Fund for Health Research, distributed to NIH institutes with small set-asides for women's health, minority health, AIDS research, and biomedical research facilities [S3].

The fund includes a dedicated allocation for efforts to reduce tobacco use and requires full funding of grants in their first year, with the money protected from ordinary budget enforcement rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would bear the cost: settlement payments of tens of billions of dollars would no longer reduce their taxable income, raising their effective cost of the settlements.

drawbacks.text: Deductibility of ordinary business expenses is the standard rule of the corporate tax code; treating settlement payments as nondeductible singles out one industry, and defenders of the settlement framework argued that making payments nondeductible would change what companies were willing to agree to pay, potentially complicating the national settlement then under negotiation [S3].

The revenue stream is conditional: the trust fund receives nothing unless tobacco companies actually make settlement payments, and the bill includes a trigger that stops all fund distributions in any year NIH appropriations fall below the prior year, so the public-health benefit depends on annual congressional choices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit was potentially large but contingent: it depended entirely on the tobacco companies paying large settlements, an outcome that itself required separate legislation. The cost fell on one industry through a tax rule change. The design was reasonable but narrow, and the bill never advanced far enough to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and one subcommittee without ever getting a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas introduced the bill on November 12, 1997, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means, Commerce, and Budget Committees, meaning three committees would each have to act on the parts in their jurisdiction [S5].
On December 9, 1997, the bill was referred to the Health and Environment Subcommittee of the Commerce Committee, its last recorded action [S5].
No further action was taken before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies came out ahead: they kept the ability to deduct their settlement payments from taxable income, and no dedicated revenue stream for NIH health research was created. The broader national tobacco settlement the bill anticipated was never enacted in that Congress either.

for.name: Rep. George W. Gekas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny tax deductions for tobacco settlement payments and route the revenue to NIH research; it attracted no cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of jurisdiction for the tax provision
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 12, 1997, and took no action; the bill was never marked up or reported

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Tobacco manufacturers facing the national settlement
against.what_they_did: Opposed tobacco-control and settlement legislation during the 1997-98 negotiations, including provisions that would have raised the cost of settlement payments

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan divide ever formed; it simply never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would have made their multibillion-dollar settlement and judgment payments nondeductible, directly raising their tax bills. The industry's interest in keeping those payments deductible ran against funding public health from the same money.
The bill created a dedicated trust fund for NIH research, including tobacco-use reduction programs, funded entirely by the revenue gained from ending the deduction.
